title: The Canticle of the Sun
hookLine: Francis, nearly blind, praises God for brother sun, sister water, even sister death

cards: A small hut stands beside a chapel in Italy, around the year 1225. Inside, a man lies in the dark. His eyes are so diseased that daylight is agony, so they've shaded him from it.

He's in constant pain and sleeps badly; tradition says the mice ran over him at night. He has given away everything he ever owned. And in that hut, half blind, sick and poor, he writes a song thanking God for the sun.
His name is Francis of Assisi. Today: Laudato si'.

teach.b: Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant. He gave it all up to live in poverty, preach, and care for lepers. By 1225 he was worn out and nearly blind, near the end of his life, when he composed this song.
Not in Latin, the church's language, but in the everyday language of his region; readers of Italian treasure it as an early poem in their language.

It begins with praise to the Most High, then goes through creation like a family roll call. Praised be you, my Lord, with all your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who brings the day. For Sister Moon and the stars.
For Brother Wind and the air.
For Sister Water, very useful and humble and precious and pure. For Brother Fire, beautiful and playful and strong. For our Sister Mother Earth, who feeds us.
Brother and sister: not resources or scenery, family. Francis isn't worshipping the sun. He's praising God for it, or through it; his little word per can mean either.
And he treats it as kin. Later he added a verse praising those who forgive for love, and the story goes that he sent friars to sing it to settle a quarrel between the bishop and the mayor of Assisi.
At the very end, knowing he was dying, he added one more: praised be you, my Lord, for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no one living can escape. Not an enemy. Family too.
He died soon after. In 2015, Pope Francis took the song's opening words, Laudato si', praised be you, as the title of his letter on caring for the earth.

how: Christians sing versions of Francis's Canticle, such as the hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King', and Franciscans pray it as part of their tradition of caring for creation.

o: a vow to give up everything you own
a prayer for healing from an illness
praised be you: Francis's song of thanks

s: Francis wrote the Canticle in Latin
he wrote it in the everyday language of his region, an early poem in Italian.
he praised God for the sun, and treated it as a brother.
he wrote it while nearly blind and ill
near the end of his life, in 1225, shaded from the daylight.

games.q: you're Francis. you're dying. the song is almost finished. what do you add?
o: a verse praising God for sister death.
games.why: he added praise for Sister Bodily Death, from whom no one living can escape. not an enemy; family.

practice: Choose one element, the sun, water or fire, and if you can, go to it: stand in a patch of light, run water over your hands, or look at a candle or a stove flame. Think of it for a moment as a brother or sister, not a thing.
If you pray, you can use Francis's words: praised be you, my Lord, for sister water.

wordCard.voice: Laudato si'. Praised be you: Francis's song thanking God for brother sun, sister water, and at the last, sister death.

orig.note: old Umbrian Italian, close to Latin: praised be you, my Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: praised be, for sister water. Sun, water, fire: kin, not scenery. Day two hundred sixty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures (Cantico di Frate Sole), c. 1225
